title: Responding to Sports Injuries: First Aid (SALTAPS & PRICE)
description: How to assess an injured performer using SALTAPS and manage soft-tissue injuries with PRICE and DRABC.
content_html:
Why First Aid Matters in Sport

Every sports session carries some risk of injury. When something goes wrong, a coach, referee or first aider must act quickly and correctly. Knowing the right assessment and treatment protocols can prevent a minor injury from becoming a serious one, and could even save a life. Two of the most important tools in sport first aid are the SALTAPS protocol and the PRICE therapy framework.

SALTAPS: The On-Field Assessment

SALTAPS is a seven-step routine for assessing an injured performer on the pitch or court. It helps the first responder gather information systematically before deciding whether the athlete can continue, needs to be removed, or requires emergency help. The steps are as follows.

See — observe the incident as it happens or arrive on the scene and look for obvious signs of injury such as unusual posture, swelling or deformity. Ask — question the performer about what happened, where it hurts and what the pain feels like; this gives subjective information that cannot be seen. Look — carry out a visual inspection of the injured area, comparing it to the uninjured side; look for swelling, bruising, redness or deformity. Touch — with the performer’s permission, gently palpate (feel) the area to identify specific points of tenderness or crepitus (a grinding sensation that may indicate a fracture).

Active movement — ask the performer to move the injured part themselves (without assistance) through their pain-free range; this tests whether the muscles and tendons are working. Passive movement — the first aider gently moves the injured joint while the performer’s muscles remain relaxed; this tests the integrity of ligaments and joint structures. Strength testing — the performer resists gentle pressure applied by the first aider; if this is pain-free and strength is maintained, return to play may be considered. If any step reveals a significant problem, the performer should be removed and further assessment arranged.

Key Fact

SALTAPS stands for See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement, Strength testing. It is the standard on-field assessment routine used to decide whether an injured performer can continue or must be removed from play.

DRABC: Emergency First Aid

If a performer is unconscious or you suspect a life-threatening emergency, SALTAPS is set aside and the DRABC protocol takes over. Danger — ensure the scene is safe for you, the performer and bystanders before approaching. Response — check for consciousness by calling the performer’s name and tapping their shoulders firmly. Airway — if unresponsive, open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin. Breathing — look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Circulation — if the performer is not breathing normally, call emergency services immediately and begin CPR at 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths.

If a performer is unconscious but breathing normally and has no life-threatening conditions, place them in the recovery position: roll them onto their side, support the head and tilt it back slightly to keep the airway clear, and ensure the top knee is bent to prevent rolling forward. Monitor their breathing continuously until emergency services arrive.

SALTAPS is for alert, conscious performers who have sustained a musculoskeletal injury such as a sprain or strain. The moment a performer is unresponsive, unconscious, not breathing normally, or you suspect cardiac arrest, DRABC must be applied immediately. Never delay DRABC to complete a SALTAPS assessment. The priority order in any emergency is always: safety first, then airway, then circulation. Calling 999 (or 112) early is critical — a defibrillator should be retrieved while CPR begins.

PRICE Therapy: Immediate Soft-Tissue Management

Once a conscious performer with a soft-tissue injury (sprain, strain or contusion) has been assessed and removed from play, PRICE therapy guides the immediate treatment. Applied within the first 24–72 hours, it limits swelling, reduces pain and creates the best conditions for healing.

Protection — protect the injury from further damage, for example by using a splint, sling or by simply stopping the performer from weight-bearing. Rest — stop physical activity to prevent aggravation; this does not mean total bed rest but avoidance of the activity that caused the injury. Ice — apply a cold pack or ice wrapped in a damp cloth for 15–20 minutes every two hours; never apply ice directly to skin as this risks an ice burn. Compression — apply a firm (but not tight) bandage to reduce swelling and provide support. Elevation — raise the injured limb above the level of the heart to reduce blood pooling and oedema.

Key Fact

PRICE stands for Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Each step targets a different aspect of the inflammatory response: protection prevents further damage, ice and compression reduce swelling, and elevation drains excess fluid away from the injury site.

X-rays and Specialist Assessment

When a fracture is suspected following the SALTAPS assessment — for example, if there is point tenderness over bone, obvious deformity or the performer cannot bear weight — the performer must be referred for an X-ray. X-rays detect whether bones are broken and whether a fracture is open or closed. You do not need to understand the technical process of how X-rays work, but you must know that they are the primary imaging tool used to diagnose skeletal injury in sport.

A very common error both in practice and in exam answers is stating that ice should be applied directly to the skin. This causes an ice burn (frostbite injury to the superficial tissues) and is incorrect. Ice must always be wrapped in a damp cloth or placed in an ice bag with a cloth barrier. Similarly, do not state that compression should be applied as tightly as possible — a bandage that is too tight can restrict circulation. If a performer’s fingers or toes become pale, cold or numb after bandaging, the bandage is too tight and must be loosened immediately.
exam_tip_html: In exam questions about SALTAPS, you will often be given a scenario describing what a first aider does and asked to name the step. Learn each letter’s meaning precisely — confusing ‘Active’ (performer moves themselves) with ‘Passive’ (first aider moves the limb) is a very common error. For PRICE questions, always state what each step achieves, not just what it involves: for example, elevation ‘reduces swelling by draining excess fluid away from the injured site’ earns more marks than simply ‘raise the leg’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SALTAPS (See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active, Passive, Strength) is the systematic on-field assessment used to decide whether an injured performer can continue; if a performer is unconscious or not breathing, switch immediately to DRABC and call 999.
  • PRICE therapy (Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) is the first-line treatment for soft-tissue injuries applied within the first 24–72 hours; ice must never be applied directly to skin.
  • An unconscious performer who is breathing should be placed in the recovery position to keep the airway clear; X-rays are used when a fracture is suspected following field assessment.

glossary_terms.definition: A seven-step on-field assessment routine used to decide whether an injured player should continue: See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement, Strength testing.
An acronym for the immediate management of soft-tissue injuries: Protection, Rest, Ice, Compress, Elevate.
An emergency first-aid checklist applied when a performer is unresponsive: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation.
A stable side-lying position used to keep the airway open in an unconscious but breathing casualty.

practice_questions.text:
In SALTAPS, what does the letter 'A' (first A) stand for?
A) Assess
B) Ask
C) Active
D) Airway
State two things a first aider should do during the 'Look' step of the SALTAPS assessment.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: visually inspect the injured area / compare to the uninjured side / look for swelling / look for bruising / look for redness / look for deformity. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why ice should not be applied directly to the skin when using PRICE therapy.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic point (1 mark): ice applied directly to skin can cause an ice burn / frostbite. Development (2 marks): the extreme cold damages the superficial skin tissues, causing a cold burn injury that could be more serious than the original soft-tissue injury. Further development with example (3 marks): add that ice must always be wrapped in a damp cloth or placed in an ice bag with a cloth barrier — for example, a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a damp tea towel applied for 15–20 minutes achieves the therapeutic cooling effect without skin damage. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the PRICE therapy protocol used to treat a sprained ankle immediately after injury. Give an example of how each step would be applied.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks (one per correctly described and exemplified step, maximum 4). Protection — e.g. prevent the performer from weight-bearing, use a support bandage or splint. Rest — e.g. remove the performer from play and stop all activity involving the ankle. Ice — e.g. apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes every two hours. Compression — e.g. apply a firm bandage around the ankle to limit swelling. Elevation — e.g. raise the ankle above hip height while the performer sits or lies down. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A rugby player is injured during a match. The physiotherapist runs onto the pitch and begins a SALTAPS assessment. The player is conscious and alert.

Discuss how the physiotherapist should carry out the SALTAPS assessment and what decisions they might make at each stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A thorough discussion covering at least four SALTAPS steps with explanation of what the physiotherapist does at each step and what the findings might indicate, including two contrasting outcomes (e.g. if active movement is pain-free the player may continue; if strength testing reveals weakness the player is removed). Some reference to decision-making based on findings.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least three steps correctly identified and explained with some decision-making discussed.
Developing (2 marks): Two or more steps identified but little explanation of process or decision-making.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point about injury assessment. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A football coach has two players injured during training: one has a suspected sprained wrist and the other is unconscious on the pitch after a collision.

Evaluate the extent to which having a clear understanding of both SALTAPS and DRABC allows a coach to manage sports injuries effectively and safely.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that explains how SALTAPS systematically assesses a conscious injured performer and supports sound return-to-play decisions, and how DRABC provides a life-saving sequence for unconscious or non-breathing performers. The response applies both protocols correctly to the scenario (sprained wrist → SALTAPS then PRICE; unconscious player → DRABC immediately, do not complete SALTAPS). A well-supported judgement is reached — e.g. that both protocols together provide comprehensive first-aid coverage, but that their effectiveness also depends on the coach’s training and calm execution under pressure.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both protocols described accurately with some applied evaluation and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): One protocol covered well, the other only briefly; limited evaluation or judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic first-aid points with no clear evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the 'P' in the PRICE acronym stand for?
In DRABC, what does the 'R' stand for?
In the SALTAPS routine, 'Passive movement' means the _____ gently moves the injured joint while the performer’s muscles remain relaxed.
Ice should always be wrapped in a _____ before being applied to an injured area to prevent an ice burn.
Match each SALTAPS step to its correct description.
right: Palpate the area to find specific points of tenderness
Performer resists gentle pressure to test muscle function
Observe the incident and look for obvious signs of injury

flashcard_questions.a: See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement, Strength testing — the seven-step on-field injury assessment routine.
Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation — the immediate treatment protocol for soft-tissue injuries.
Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation — the emergency first-aid sequence for an unresponsive performer.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between active and passive movement in SALTAPS?
flashcard_questions.a: Active movement is performed by the athlete alone; passive movement is the first aider moving the joint while the athlete’s muscles stay relaxed.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must ice never be applied directly to skin?
flashcard_questions.a: Direct ice contact causes an ice burn (frostbite) to the superficial skin tissues, which can be more harmful than the original injury.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of the Elevation step in PRICE?
flashcard_questions.a: Raising the injured limb above heart level reduces blood pooling and drains excess fluid away from the injury site.

flashcard_questions.q: When should a first aider switch from SALTAPS to DRABC?
flashcard_questions.a: Immediately if the performer becomes unresponsive, stops breathing normally, or any life-threatening emergency is suspected.

flashcard_questions.q: What position should an unconscious but breathing performer be placed in?
flashcard_questions.a: The recovery position — lying on their side with the head tilted back slightly to keep the airway clear and open.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the ‘Touch’ step of SALTAPS involve?
flashcard_questions.a: The first aider gently palpates the injured area to identify specific points of tenderness or signs of possible fracture.

flashcard_questions.q: When is an X-ray used following an on-field injury assessment?
flashcard_questions.a: When a fracture is suspected — for example, if there is bony tenderness, visible deformity, or the performer cannot bear weight.

flashcard_questions.q: How long and how often should ice be applied during PRICE therapy?
flashcard_questions.a: For 15 to 20 minutes every two hours during the first 24 to 72 hours after the injury occurs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of the Compression step in PRICE?
flashcard_questions.a: A firm bandage is applied to limit swelling and provide support, but it must not restrict circulation to the limb.
